t: The instructions for making you are locked in a room. So how does anything get built?
Every instruction for building you sits in one locked room in each cell. The builders are outside. How does the message get out?
The genome never leaves the nucleus. Protein synthesis happens outside it. Something has to carry the message across.
Compartmentalisation separates the archive from the factory. That separation is not an inconvenience; it is what makes regulation possible.
sub: A copy goes out. The original never leaves.
A copy is made and sent out. The original stays where it is safe.
A transcript is made and exported. The template is never risked.
Transcription decouples the durable archive from the disposable working copy, so expression can be regulated per copy rather than per gene.

t: The locked room is the nucleus. The copy is called mRNA.
The locked room is the nucleus, the copy is messenger RNA, and the builder is a ribosome.
Transcription copies a gene into mRNA inside the nucleus; translation reads that mRNA into protein at a ribosome outside it.
Transcription produces a processed mRNA; translation decodes it in triplets at the ribosome, with tRNA as the physical adaptor between codon and amino acid.
sub: One room, one copy, one builder. That is how everything in you gets made.
Every protein in your body was made this way, right now, thousands of times a second.
This pipeline runs continuously in every cell you have, and its regulation is most of what makes a liver cell different from a neuron.
The same genome, differently transcribed. Cell identity is a statement about which genes are being read, not about which genes are present.

t: Some medicines work by sending the cell a message of our own.
An mRNA vaccine works by handing your cells a copy of an instruction, which they read and then throw away.
mRNA vaccines exploit exactly this pipeline: a synthetic transcript is delivered, translated into one viral protein, and degraded. The nucleus is never involved and the genome is never touched.
Delivering a transcript rather than a gene means no nuclear entry and no integration risk, which is why the platform moved so quickly through safety review.

q: Why does the original stay in its room?
Why does DNA never leave the nucleus?
Why is the template retained rather than exported?
What is the functional argument for sequestering the template?
options: So it cannot be damaged or lost
why: There is only one original. If it were damaged, every copy after it would be wrong too.
You have one copy of your genome per cell. Damage to it is permanent and inherited by every daughter cell; damage to a transcript costs nothing.
The template is irreplaceable and its errors propagate; transcripts are disposable and their errors do not. Sequestering the template also allows expression to be regulated at the point of copying.
Error in a transcript is transient; error in the template is heritable. Compartmentalisation also creates a regulatory step between archive and product.

q: What does the builder need before it can build?
What does a ribosome need before it can make anything?
What are the minimum inputs to translation?
What does a ribosome require beyond a transcript?
why: A builder with no instructions builds nothing. The copy has to arrive first.
A ribosome is a reader. Without a transcript to read it has no sequence to follow, however much energy is available.
Translation needs the transcript, charged tRNAs and GTP. The transcript is what makes the product specific — the rest is machinery.
Machinery plus energy yields nothing without sequence information. Specificity enters only through the transcript.
